title: The macro-enabled invoice — question explanation
learningObjective: Avoid enabling active content in untrusted documents and verify the sender
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics video; narration; separate captions; no autoplay with sound
visualStyle: Deep navy and charcoal; restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights; limited purple accents; clean typography; purposeful, low-motion transitions; accessible contrast.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: A supplier sends an invoice document you were not expecting. When opened in a preview, it asks you to “Enable Content” to display the invoice.
scenes.direction: Show a fictional simulated setting. Use generic UI and no actual organization, brand, user identity, credential, real URL or live account.

scenes.name: Learning objective and risk cue
scenes.visual: Avoid enabling active content in untrusted documents and verify the sender
scenes.direction: Highlight only observable cues and explain the decision context without implying certainty beyond the scenario.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option B: Verify the invoice with the supplier through known contact details and report the suspicious request; do not enable content. Unexpected documents and requests to enable active content require independent verification.
scenes.direction: Animate the recommended defensive choice as a clear decision path. Display the action verb and trusted channel/control.

scenes.name: Why the other options fail
scenes.visual: Option A: Disconnecting does not make untrusted active content safe; it may still alter or persist on the device. Option C: Uploading a business document publicly may disclose confidential data; use organization-approved analysis channels. Option D: Unexpected active content can execute code and should not be enabled simply to view a document.
scenes.direction: Show each unsafe alternative separately with a complete, concise reason. Do not depict operational exploitation, malicious code or credential capture.

scenes.name: Defensive takeaway
scenes.visual: Close the document without enabling content. Verify with the supplier using a known contact method and use approved security analysis if needed. Do not enable macros or active content in an unexpected document to reveal what it contains.
scenes.direction: Close with one readable takeaway and the next safe action. Keep the final frame long enough for comprehension.
scenes.onScreenText: Do not enable macros or active content in an unexpected document to reveal what it contains.

narration: Scenario: A supplier sends an invoice document you were not expecting. When opened in a preview, it asks you to “Enable Content” to display the invoice. Safest response: Option B: Verify the invoice with the supplier through known contact details and report the suspicious request; do not enable content. Unexpected documents and requests to enable active content require independent verification. Option A is unsafe because Disconnecting does not make untrusted active content safe; it may still alter or persist on the device. Option C is unsafe because Uploading a business document publicly may disclose confidential data; use organization-approved analysis channels. Option D is unsafe because Unexpected active content can execute code and should not be enabled simply to view a document. In practice: Close the document without enabling content. Verify with the supplier using a known contact method and use approved security analysis if needed. Key takeaway: Do not enable macros or active content in an unexpected document to reveal what it contains.
